title: Streaming and latency
summary: Why AI answers appear word by word, how to stream them through your own server, and what to do when a job is too slow for one request.
youWillLearn: Why time to first token matters more to users than total time
How a streamed answer travels from the model, through your route, to the browser
Which timeouts sit in that chain, and who sets them
When to stop streaming and move work into a background job

glossary.latency: How long someone waits between asking and getting a result.
glossary.streaming: Sending a response in small pieces as it is produced, instead of all at once at the end.
glossary.time to first token: How long until the first piece of the answer arrives. It decides whether an app feels fast.
glossary.SSE: Server-sent events: a simple web standard where the server keeps one response open and pushes small text events down it.
glossary.timeout: A limit on how long something may run or wait. When it is hit, the work is cut off with an error.
glossary.background job: Work that runs outside the user's request, so the request can answer right away and the result arrives later.
glossary.polling: The browser asking again every few seconds: is it done yet?
glossary.abort: Cancelling a request that is still running, so neither side keeps working on it.

steps.title: Twenty seconds of spinner
body: Maya clicks AI summary on a long note. A spinner turns. And turns. After twenty seconds the full summary pops in at once.

Nothing is broken. The model was writing the whole time, one token after another. Notely waited for the very last token before showing anything. To Maya, that latency looks like a frozen app, and she clicks again.

scene.caption: The server waits for the complete answer. The browser sees nothing until the end.

steps.title: Show the words as they are written
body: The fix is streaming: pass each piece along the moment it exists. The total time barely changes. What changes is the time to first token: Maya sees words within a second or two, and reading keeps pace with writing.
This is why every AI chat types its answer out. It is not a visual effect; it is the real speed of generation.

callout.text: A waiter who brings each dish as it is ready, instead of holding the whole order until dessert is done. The meal takes as long; nobody sits hungry.

scene.caption: Tokens flow through the server to the browser as soon as they exist.

steps.title: One response that stays open
body: With streaming on, the Claude API keeps the HTTP response open and sends a series of small events. This format is called SSE.

First a message_start, then many content_block_delta events, each carrying a few characters of text, then message_stop. A few bookkeeping events sit in between. The SDK turns these into simple callbacks, so you rarely read the raw format, but you will see it in network logs.

code.caption: Shortened. Each event is a line of JSON pushed down the same open response.

scene.caption: One open response from the API, carrying many small events.

steps.title: Your route passes the stream along
body: The browser never talks to the model directly, so your route must relay the stream. It opens a stream to the API, and returns its own streaming response to the browser.
On the page, the code reads that response chunk by chunk and appends text to the summary box. Many teams use a helper library for this; the plumbing underneath is the same.

code.caption: The route reads the note itself, by id, for the logged-in user. It never trusts note text sent by the browser.

scene.caption: Two streams joined end to end: API to route, route to browser.

steps.title: A chain of timeouts
body: Every hop has a timeout. The browser's fetch can give up. Your serverless function has a maximum run time set by the host and your plan. The SDK has its own request timeout.
The shortest one wins. A long answer can be cut off by your function's limit even while the model is still writing happily.

callout.text: On Vercel, a route can raise its own limit with export const maxDuration = 60 (seconds), up to what your plan allows. Check the current limits in the docs rather than trusting an old blog post.

scene.caption: Each hop has its own time limit. The shortest one decides.

steps.title: Too slow for a request: background it
body: Some jobs take minutes: summarizing all of Maya's notes, or importing 500 files. No user should hold a request open that long.
So the route answers right away with 202 Accepted and a job id. A background job does the work, saves the result to a jobs table, and the page finds out by polling or a realtime subscription.

callout.text: You met queues and workers in system design. Same pattern here: the model call is the slow worker step.

scene.caption: The request returns at once. A worker does the slow part and saves the result.

steps.title: Notely: stream or background?
body: Ask one question: is a person watching and waiting for this exact answer?

Yes, and it takes seconds: stream it. The note summary and the chat reply. No, or it takes minutes: background it. The weekly digest email and the bulk import. Save every result to the database either way, so a refresh does not lose it.

callout.text: Ask: is stream used for user-facing answers? What is the route's maxDuration, and can the slowest case finish inside it? Is the finished text saved to the database? For long jobs, is there a status row, and what does the UI show while it runs or if it fails?

scene.caption: Waiting person and seconds: stream. Nobody waiting or minutes: background job.

steps.title: Streams can break halfway
body: Once streaming starts, your route has already sent 200 OK. If the API fails mid-answer, the error arrives inside the stream, so the page must handle it and show a retry.
The opposite case costs money: Maya closes the tab, but your route keeps reading tokens nobody will see. Pass the request's abort signal through, so the model call stops too.

code.caption: When the browser goes away, cancel the upstream call.

scene.caption: The tab is closed, but the model keeps writing and you keep paying.

steps.title: Recap in one breath
body: Models write one token at a time, so a full answer takes a while. Streaming does not make it faster; it makes the first words arrive early.

Relay the stream through your own route, know the shortest timeout in the chain, abort when the user leaves, and save the final text. If a job takes minutes, answer at once and do it in the background.

quiz.question: A client says: "Streaming will make our AI answers finish faster, right?" What is the honest answer?

options.text: Yes, streaming uses a faster connection to the model.
options.why: The model generates at the same speed either way. Streaming changes when you see the text, not how fast it is written.

options.text: No. Total time is about the same, but the first words show up much sooner.
options.why: Streaming cuts time to first token. Users read as the model writes, so the app feels fast even when the full answer takes as long.

options.text: No, streaming makes answers slower because of the extra events.
options.why: The event overhead is tiny. The big effect is that users see progress almost immediately.

quiz.question: Notely's new "summarize all my notes" feature fails for heavy users with a function timeout. What is the best fix?

options.text: Turn on streaming for that route.
options.why: Streaming still keeps the function running until the last token. A job of several minutes can still pass the host's limit.

options.text: Retry the request automatically until it works.
options.why: The job takes as long every time, so it will time out every time, and each retry costs tokens.

options.text: Return a job id right away and run the work in a background job.
options.why: Nobody is waiting on that exact second. A worker can take minutes, save the result, and the page picks it up when it is done.

quiz.question: Logs show many summaries that finish generating after users already left the page. What should Claude Code add?

options.text: Cancel the upstream API call when the browser's request is aborted.
options.why: Passing the abort signal through stops the model from writing tokens nobody will read, which saves money.

options.text: A loading spinner so users stay on the page.
options.why: Users will always leave sometimes. The server still needs to stop work it no longer needs.
That lets answers grow longer, which makes the waste worse, not better.

takeaways: Streaming cuts time to first token. It does not make the model write faster.
The browser talks to your route, and your route relays the model's stream. The key never leaves the server.
Every hop has a timeout; the shortest one wins. Know your function's maxDuration.
Abort the model call when the user leaves, and save the final text to the database.
If a job takes minutes, return a job id and run it as a background job.
